title: 6 Best Generator Transfer Switch Picks (2026): Kits and Inlets
description: The Reliance 31406CRK 30-amp kit is the generator transfer switch most homes need for an L14-30 generator; 6 Reliance parts, furnace switch to inlet box.
dek: The Reliance 31406CRK 30-amp kit is the generator transfer switch most homes need for an L14-30 generator; 6 Reliance parts, furnace switch to inlet box.
intro: The best generator transfer switch for most people in 2026 is the **[Reliance Controls 31406CRK Pro/Tran Manual Transfer Switch Kit](/gear/reliance-31406crk/)**. The default answer for a 5,000 to 7,500 watt portable generator with an L14-30 outlet and a short list of must-run circuits.

A transfer switch is what turns a portable generator into backup power for your furnace, well pump and fridge without endangering the people fixing the lines. Six parts matched to the job, plus how to choose between a switch and an interlock.

Every outage season, someone plugs a generator into a dryer outlet with a homemade cord and energizes the line a utility crew is working on. A transfer switch exists so that never happens, and the right one for most homes is a modest kit plus a few hours of an electrician's time.
quickAnswer: The Reliance Controls 31406CRK Pro/Tran Manual Transfer Switch Kit is our #1 pick (best overall transfer switch). The default answer for a 5,000 to 7,500 watt portable generator with an L14-30 outlet and a short list of must-run circuits.

picks.label: Best Overall Transfer Switch
writeup: The 31406CRK is the transfer switch most electricians reach for when a homeowner shows up with a portable generator and asks for a safe way to connect it. Reliance builds it as a small prewired panel that mounts beside your main breaker panel, with a flexible conduit whip that enters the panel through a knockout. Six chosen circuits are moved onto it, and each gets a three-position switch: Line, Off and Gen. Because every circuit is switched individually, power from the generator can only go to those circuits and never back out onto the utility lines. The CRK suffix means the kit version, which adds Reliance's PB30 outdoor power inlet box and a 30-amp generator cord, so you plug the generator into the outside wall rather than running cords through a window. It is rated for 30-amp, 120/240-volt generators with an L14-30 outlet. Six circuits is enough for a furnace, refrigerator, freezer, sump pump and a couple of lighting or outlet circuits in a typical home.
pros: Six selectable circuits covers the essentials in most houses
Each circuit has its own Line/Off/Gen switch, so you cannot energize the utility lines by design
Kit format bundles the PB30 inlet box and a 30-amp cord
Pre-wired whip shortens the electrician's install time
Pairs with the most common portable generator outlet, the L14-30
cons: Six circuits fills up fast once 240-volt loads take two positions
Still needs a licensed electrician and usually a permit

picks.label: Best for More Circuits
writeup: The 31410CRK is the ten-circuit sibling of the 31406CRK, built the same way: a prewired switch panel that sits next to your main panel, a whip into the panel, and a separate Line/Off/Gen switch for every circuit you move across. The reason to pay more is not power. Both kits are 30-amp, 120/240-volt units, and your generator's running watts still decide how much you can run at once. The reason is positions. A 240-volt load such as a well pump uses two of them, and once you add a furnace, refrigerator, freezer, sump pump, kitchen outlets and some lighting, six positions are gone before you get to the home office or the garage door opener. Ten positions also give you more freedom to balance 120-volt loads across the two legs of the generator, which keeps one side from overloading while the other loafs. Like the six-circuit kit, the CRK version adds the PB30 inlet box and a 30-amp cord.
pros: Ten circuit positions leaves room for 240-volt loads like a well pump
Same per-circuit Line/Off/Gen switching as the six-circuit model
Kit includes the PB30 inlet box and a 30-amp cord
Lets you split loads across both legs of the generator more evenly
Worth the step up when the six-circuit list is already full
cons: More circuits does not mean more power; the generator is still the limit
Larger enclosure needs more wall space next to the panel
Easy to over-wire circuits you will never run at once

picks.label: Best Transfer Switch for Furnace
writeup: In cold climates the most important load in an outage is usually the gas or oil furnace, which needs only a few hundred watts for its blower, inducer and controls but needs it hardwired. The TF151W exists for exactly that. It is a single-circuit, 15-amp, 120-volt transfer switch that replaces or sits beside the furnace's service switch, so the furnace can run either from its normal circuit or from a generator connected to the switch. There is no need to move circuits at the main panel and no need for a 240-volt generator, which makes it a good match for a small inverter generator. That is also its limit: it powers the furnace and nothing else. If you also want the refrigerator, freezer and sump pump, a six-circuit switch like the 31406CRK covers the furnace and those loads together, and costs less than buying several single-circuit switches. Have an electrician confirm it suits your furnace and local code.
pros: Purpose-built for one job: running a gas or oil furnace on a generator
Mounts at the furnace instead of at the main panel
Simple switch between utility and generator power
Far less money and labor than a whole panel switch
Works with smaller generators and inverter generators
cons: Your refrigerator, sump pump and lights still need another plan
Some furnaces are fussy about generator power quality and grounding

picks.label: Best 30-Amp Generator Inlet Box
writeup: A power inlet box is the part of a generator hookup that lives outside: a weatherproof box on the wall with a male inlet where the generator cord plugs in. The PB30 is Reliance's 30-amp version, with an L14-30 inlet that mates with the matching connector on a standard 30-amp, four-wire generator cord. Inside the house it is wired to either a manual transfer switch or, with an interlock kit, a dedicated generator breaker in the main panel. If you buy a Reliance CRK kit you already have one, so do not buy it twice. Where it earns its own place in this list is the interlock route: interlock kits supply the panel hardware, not the inlet, so you need an inlet box regardless. Mount it where the generator can sit outdoors well away from windows, doors and vents, and keep the cord run reasonably short. The male inlet cannot be energized unless the cord is connected to a running generator, which is exactly why the inlet is male and the cord end is female.
pros: Lets the generator plug in at an outside wall, not through a window
Standard L14-30 inlet matches most mid-size portables
Weatherproof enclosure with a hinged cover
Works with manual transfer switches and listed interlock kits alike
Same box the Reliance CRK kits include
cons: Only half of the system; it does nothing without a switch or interlock
Buy it separately only if your switch kit does not already include one
Needs wiring back to the switch by an electrician

picks.label: Best 50-Amp Generator Inlet Box
writeup: Large portable generators, usually around 9,000 running watts and up, often carry a 50-amp, 125/250-volt California-style twist-lock outlet alongside or instead of the L14-30. The PBN50 is Reliance's inlet box for that connection. On paper a 50-amp, 240-volt circuit can carry up to 12,000 watts, which is enough to run central air on a large portable or several big loads at once, but only if the whole path is rated for it: generator outlet, cord, inlet, wiring and the switch or interlock breaker. A 50-amp inlet feeding a 30-amp switch gains you nothing. That makes the PBN50 most useful with a panel interlock, where the generator breaker can be sized to the generator, or with a 50-amp-rated transfer switch. Check the generator's outlet before buying, because a 50-amp cord will not mate with an L14-30 outlet, and adapters that change amperage are a bad idea on a circuit like this.

Lets an interlock or 50-amp switch use the generator's full output
Weatherproof outdoor enclosure
Same male-inlet safety logic as the 30-amp box
Future-proofs the wall if you may buy a bigger generator
cons: Pointless with a generator that only has an L14-30
Needs heavier wire, which means more install cost
50-amp cords are thick, heavy and expensive

picks.label: Best Generator Cord
writeup: Most transfer switch kits include a 10-foot cord, which is often too short to put the generator where it should be: outdoors, well clear of windows, doors, vents and the garage. The PC3020 is Reliance's 20-foot, 30-amp generator cord, with an L14-30 plug at the generator end and a matching L14-30 connector at the inlet end. It is a four-conductor cord, which a 120/240-volt hookup needs, and the twist-lock ends hold firmly. A cord like this is also the honest answer to the most dangerous question in generator ownership, which is whether you can just make a cord with two male ends and plug it into a dryer outlet. You cannot. A cord with a female end at the house and a male inlet on the wall is the safe version of that idea. If you need more distance than 20 feet, ask your electrician whether a longer 30-amp cord or a relocated inlet makes more sense, because voltage drop rises with length and thin cords overheat.

Twist-lock ends do not pull out under their own weight
Made by the same company as the inlet box

sections.h: What a Generator Transfer Switch Does, and Why You Need One

blocks.p: A portable generator makes useful power, but it has no safe way to reach the furnace, the well pump or the refrigerator's dedicated circuit on its own. Extension cords cover a few plug-in appliances and nothing hardwired. A generator transfer switch is the piece that connects the generator to selected household circuits while guaranteeing those circuits are disconnected from the utility at the same moment. That last part is the whole point, and it is why a transfer switch or a listed interlock is required by the National Electrical Code for any generator connected to premises wiring.

The reason is simple and deadly. If generator power flows into your panel while the main breaker is on, it runs backward out to the street, through the pole transformer, and steps up to thousands of volts on the line a utility crew believes is dead. That is backfeeding, and it kills lineworkers and neighbors every year. It also lets utility power slam into your generator when the grid comes back, which can destroy the generator or start a fire. The so-called suicide cord, a cord with two male plugs used to feed a dryer or range outlet, is the classic way people do it. Never use one, under any circumstances.

A properly installed transfer switch makes that impossible by design. Each switched circuit can be connected to the utility or to the generator, never both. Manual switches do it with a physical switch per circuit; interlock kits do it with a sliding plate that blocks the main breaker and the generator breaker from being on together; automatic switches do it with a motorized mechanism. All three are legitimate when installed correctly and listed for the job. What is not legitimate is anything that relies on you remembering to flip the main breaker first.

A transfer switch also makes outages calmer. Instead of snaking cords through a cracked window, which lets exhaust in, you roll the generator out, plug one cord into an inlet box on the wall, start it, and move a few switches. Your furnace runs, your sump pump runs, your lights work on their normal switches. The generator itself still has to run outdoors, far from openings, and you still need working carbon monoxide alarms inside. A transfer switch fixes the wiring problem, not the exhaust problem.

If you have not yet chosen a generator, start with our pillar guide to the [best home generators for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/), then come back here. The switch has to match the generator's outlet and output, so picking the generator first saves buying the wrong kit.

sections.h: Manual Transfer Switch vs Interlock Kit vs Automatic

blocks.p: A manual transfer switch, the kind Reliance sells as Pro/Tran, is a small prewired subpanel that mounts beside your main panel. An electrician moves your chosen circuits onto it, and each one gets its own Line/Off/Gen switch. During an outage you plug in the generator, start it, and flip only the circuits you want onto generator power. It is the most foolproof option for owners who will use it a few times a year, because you can see exactly which circuits are on the generator and cannot accidentally feed the whole house.

An interlock kit takes a different approach. It is a metal plate or slide mounted on the main panel's cover that physically prevents the main breaker and a dedicated generator breaker from being on at the same time. The generator feeds the panel through that breaker from an outdoor inlet box. Because the whole panel becomes available, you manage loads by switching off the branch breakers you do not want and turning on the ones you do. Interlocks are usually cheaper than a manual switch and offer every circuit, but they demand more discipline during an outage.

The catch with interlocks is that they must be listed for your specific panel. Interlocks are not universal: the plate has to fit the exact panel model, breaker layout and cover, and the generator breaker must be secured as the listing requires. Panel manufacturers sell their own interlock kits for some models, and third-party kits are sold for others. An electrician will check the panel's label and the local inspector's position before installing one. Some jurisdictions are stricter about third-party interlocks than others, so ask before buying anything.

An automatic transfer switch senses the outage, starts a standby generator, and moves the load without anyone touching it. That is the right answer for permanently installed home standby generators and for people who travel or have medical equipment that cannot wait. For a portable generator that has to be wheeled out and started by hand, automatic switching mostly adds cost without adding much. If you are leaning toward a standby system, our breakdown of [what a Generac standby installation costs](/generac-generator-cost/) includes the transfer switch in the total.

sections.h: 30-Amp L14-30 vs 50-Amp: Matching the Switch to the Generator

blocks.p: The first spec to check on any generator transfer switch is the inlet and amperage, and that is decided by your generator's largest outlet. Most portable generators in the 5,000 to 9,000 watt range have a NEMA L14-30 outlet: a 30-amp, 120/240-volt, four-prong twist-lock. Larger portables often add a 50-amp, 125/250-volt California-style outlet, sometimes called a CS6369 outlet, that takes a cord with a CS6365 plug. Look at the generator's control panel; the outlet type is printed beside it.

The amperage sets the ceiling. A 30-amp, 240-volt connection can carry about 7,200 watts in theory, and 30-amp switch kits like Reliance's are generally marketed for generators up to about 7,500 running watts. A 50-amp, 240-volt connection can carry up to 12,000 watts. In practice you should plan to run well under the ceiling, because motor starts surge far above running watts and generators do not like sitting at their limit for hours. Buying a 50-amp inlet for a generator with only an L14-30 outlet gains you nothing.

Watch out for generators that are 120-volt only. Some smaller portables and many inverter generators have only 120-volt outlets, sometimes including an L5-30 or an RV-style TT-30. Those cannot feed both legs of a standard 120/240-volt switch the way an L14-30 can, and they cannot run any 240-volt load at all. Do not let anyone jumper the two legs together to make it work. A single-circuit furnace switch suits that kind of generator better, or talk to an electrician about what is allowed.

The cord has to match both ends. A 30-amp system uses an L14-30 plug at the generator and an L14-30 connector at the inlet, on a four-wire cord with 10-gauge conductors. A 50-amp system uses a much heavier cord. Adapters that turn a 50-amp outlet into a 30-amp cord exist, but they put you in a position where the cord and inlet are protected only by the generator's own breaker, so ask your electrician before using one.
THE RULE
Match the inlet to the generator's biggest 240-volt outlet.
L14-30 on the generator means a 30-amp inlet and switch. A 50-amp CS6369 outlet means a 50-amp inlet is worth considering, but only if the switch or interlock breaker is sized to use it.

sections.h: Transfer Switch for Furnace: The Single-Circuit Option

blocks.p: If the only thing you truly need in a winter outage is heat, a transfer switch for furnace use is the simplest legitimate setup. A gas or oil furnace with a blower, inducer motor, igniter and control board typically needs a few hundred watts running, more at blower start. That is within reach of even a small inverter generator. The problem has never been power; it is that the furnace is hardwired, so there is nowhere safe to plug a generator in.

A furnace transfer switch like the Reliance TF151W solves that at the furnace itself. It replaces or sits beside the furnace's service switch, and lets you flip the furnace from its normal circuit to a generator connection. No panel work, no 240-volt generator, and a much smaller electrician bill. People sometimes ask whether they can just put a plug on the furnace and use an extension cord. Some jurisdictions allow a cord-and-plug furnace connection and many do not, and the answer depends on the furnace's installation instructions, so let an electrician decide rather than improvising.

Furnaces can be particular about generator power. Modern control boards sense the flame through a small current that depends on a solid neutral-to-ground reference, and some furnaces refuse to light on a generator with a floating neutral or with reversed polarity. Inverter generators produce clean power, which helps electronics, but the grounding question is separate. If the furnace locks out on generator power, that is an electrician's diagnosis, not a reason to start modifying cords or bonding plugs yourself.

A furnace-only switch is a narrow tool. It keeps the heat on, but the refrigerator, freezer, sump pump and lights still need another answer. If you want two or three of those as well, a six-circuit switch like the 31406CRK usually makes more sense than multiple single-circuit switches. If you are also looking at plug-in heat as a backup, our guide to the [best indoor heaters for a power outage](/best-indoor-heater-for-power-outage/) covers what is actually safe to run inside.

sections.h: Load Management: Choosing Which Circuits Go on the Generator

blocks.p: A transfer switch does not make the generator any bigger. Whether you choose six circuits, ten, or the whole panel through an interlock, the generator's running watts decide what can run at the same moment. The job is to pick circuits that matter in an outage and that the generator can actually start. A furnace, refrigerator, freezer, sump pump, a few lighting circuits and the circuit that feeds your internet router cover most households.

Start with the loads that cannot wait. A sump pump in a wet basement and a well pump in a rural house come first, then refrigeration, then heat, then lighting and communications. Well pumps and many sump pumps have large starting surges, so check the motor's rating plate or ask a pump installer. Our guide to the [best generator for a well pump](/best-generator-for-well-pump/) walks through starting-watt math for 240-volt submersibles in detail.

Leave the heavy resistive loads off. An electric water heater, electric range, electric dryer and central air conditioner can each swallow most or all of a portable generator's output. Putting them on the switch invites someone to turn them on mid-outage and trip the generator. If you want to know what your house actually draws, a whole-home energy monitor gives you real numbers instead of nameplate guesses.

Balance the two legs. A 120/240-volt generator delivers half its capacity on each 120-volt leg, so putting the furnace, refrigerator and freezer all on the same leg can overload that side while the other runs light. Electricians plan this when they assign circuits to the switch, and it is one of the better reasons to have a professional do the layout. Before the electrician arrives, use a circuit breaker finder to label your panel properly, which makes the circuit-selection conversation far faster.

sections.h: Electrician, Permit and Inspection: How Installation Works

blocks.p: Installing a generator transfer switch is panel work, and panel work belongs to a licensed electrician. The main lugs in your panel stay energized even with the main breaker off, the service conductors upstream of the main have no protection at all, and a mistake can leave a switch that looks right but backfeeds. Most jurisdictions require a permit for the work and an inspection afterward, and your homeowner's insurance may care whether you have one if anything ever goes wrong.

A typical manual switch install goes like this. The electrician mounts the switch beside the main panel, runs its whip into a knockout, moves your chosen branch circuits onto the switch, mounts the inlet box on an outside wall, and runs cable between the two. An interlock install involves fitting the listed plate, installing the generator breaker, and running cable from the inlet box to that breaker. Either way, it is commonly a half-day job for a straightforward panel, longer if the inlet is far from the panel.

Expect the electrician to ask about your generator. They need to know its outlet type, its running watts, and whether its neutral is bonded to the frame. Many portables ship with a bonded neutral, and some transfer switches do not switch the neutral, which can create a second neutral-to-ground bond and cause GFCI trips. The fix depends on the generator and the switch, and it is an electrician's call. Do not remove bonding straps or modify the generator yourself.

Some utilities also want to know you have a generator connected to your house. It costs nothing to ask, and in some areas it is required. While the electrician is there, it is worth adding a [whole-house surge protector](/best-whole-house-surge-protector/), since the panel is already open and generator power and grid restoration are both sources of voltage swings.
NEVER
Never backfeed through a dryer or range outlet.

A cord with male plugs on both ends energizes the utility lines and can kill a lineworker. It also leaves exposed live prongs on the loose end. No outage is worth it. If you need power before an electrician can come, run cords to individual appliances from a generator placed safely outdoors.

sections.h: Operating the Switch Safely During an Outage

blocks.p: The order matters, and it is worth taping a card with it inside the panel door. Set up the generator outdoors, far from windows, doors and vents, with the exhaust pointed away from the house. Connect the cord to the generator and then to the inlet box. Start the generator and let it warm up for a minute or two. Then switch circuits from Line to Gen one at a time, starting with the biggest motor load, so each start surge happens on its own instead of all at once.

With an interlock, the sequence is a bit different. Turn off the main breaker, slide the interlock plate, and turn on the generator breaker. Then turn off most branch breakers and bring circuits back on one by one, watching the generator's load. This is where interlocks need more care than a manual switch: everything in the panel is available, so it is easy to switch on a water heater or dryer circuit by habit. Some owners label the must-run breakers in a bright color.

When the grid comes back, reverse the process. Move each circuit back to Line, or turn off the generator breaker and slide the interlock back to restore the main, then shut down the generator and let it cool before unplugging. Never refuel a running or hot generator, and store fuel in approved containers away from the house. If you use a pump to move fuel from cans, our guide to the [best fuel transfer pumps](/best-fuel-transfer-pump/) covers the types that suit gasoline.

Generator placement is not optional. Carbon monoxide from a portable generator in a garage, crawlspace or on a porch kills people every outage season, even with doors open. Keep the generator outdoors and well away from the house, and have battery-backed CO alarms on every level. If you need power for medical equipment inside, a battery system such as those in our [portable power station for home backup](/best-portable-power-station-for-home-backup/) guide can bridge the gap safely indoors.

sections.h: Which Generator Transfer Switch to Buy

blocks.p: If you have a portable generator with an L14-30 outlet and a short list of essentials, buy the Reliance 31406CRK. It covers six circuits, includes the inlet box and a cord, and is the setup most electricians already know how to install. For most houses with a gas furnace, a refrigerator, a freezer and a sump pump, six positions is enough.

If your list includes a 240-volt well pump or runs past six circuits, step up to the Reliance 31410CRK. The power ceiling is the same; the extra positions are what you are paying for. If your only real need is heat and your generator is small or 120-volt only, the Reliance TF151W furnace switch is the cheapest legitimate route, as long as your furnace and local code accept it.

If your electrician recommends an interlock for your panel, buy the interlock kit listed for that exact panel, plus the Reliance PB30 inlet box for a 30-amp generator or the PBN50 for a generator with a 50-amp outlet. Add the Reliance PC3020 cord when the 10-foot kit cord does not let you place the generator safely away from the house.

Whatever you buy, budget for the electrician and permit, because they are not optional extras; they are what makes the hardware safe. And if you are still deciding on the generator, our pages on the [best gas generators](/best-gas-generator/) and the [best small generators for home](/best-small-generator-for-home/) cover the models that pair well with each switch.

mistakes: Using a double-male cord into a dryer outlet

A suicide cord feeds generator power backward into the utility lines, where it can kill a lineworker, and leaves live exposed prongs on the free end. It is illegal and indefensible. If no transfer switch is installed yet, run extension cords to individual appliances instead, with the generator outdoors and well away from openings.
Buying an interlock not listed for your panel

Interlock kits are panel-specific. A plate that fits a different panel model, or a universal kit an inspector will not accept, can fail inspection or fail to prevent both breakers being on. Have your electrician read the panel label and choose a kit listed for that exact panel before you order anything.
Expecting more circuits to mean more power

A ten-circuit switch does not make a 7,500-watt generator any stronger. The generator's running watts still decide what can run together. Choose circuits by priority, keep big resistive loads like water heaters off the switch, and stagger motor starts so the generator is not hit with every surge at once.
Buying a 50-amp inlet for a 30-amp generator

The inlet should match the generator's largest 240-volt outlet. If the generator only has an L14-30, a 50-amp inlet box and cord add cost and weight without adding any usable power. Buy the 30-amp PB30 setup unless the generator actually has a 50-amp outlet and the switch can use it.

Transfer switch installs involve the main panel, where some parts stay live even with the main off. A licensed electrician, a permit and an inspection are what make the system safe and insurable. DIY installs that look fine can still backfeed or create grounding faults that only show up during an outage.
bottomLine: For most homes with a portable generator and an L14-30 outlet, the Reliance 31406CRK is the right generator transfer switch: six circuits, an inlet box and a cord in one kit. Step up to the 31410CRK for a well pump or a longer list, or choose the TF151W if keeping the furnace running is all you need. Whatever you choose, have a licensed electrician install it with a permit, keep the generator outdoors and away from openings, and never, ever backfeed through an outlet.

faqs.q: Do I need a transfer switch for a portable generator?
faqs.a: You need one if you want the generator to power anything hardwired, such as a furnace, well pump or the circuits in your panel. The National Electrical Code requires a transfer switch or listed interlock for any generator connected to household wiring. If you only plan to run a refrigerator and a few lamps on extension cords plugged directly into the generator, a transfer switch is not required, but it is far more convenient and safer.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a transfer switch and an interlock kit?
faqs.a: A manual transfer switch is a small prewired panel with its own switch for each chosen circuit, mounted beside the main panel. An interlock kit is a plate on the main panel that prevents the main breaker and a generator breaker from being on together, which makes the whole panel available. Interlocks usually cost less but must be listed for your specific panel, and you manage loads by switching breakers yourself.

faqs.q: Can I install a generator transfer switch myself?
faqs.a: In most places this is work for a licensed electrician, with a permit and inspection. It involves the main panel, where the incoming service conductors stay energized even with the main breaker off. Some jurisdictions allow homeowners to do electrical work on their own home with a permit, but transfer switches are a poor place to learn, because an error can backfeed the utility lines or create a fire hazard.

faqs.q: What size transfer switch do I need?
faqs.a: Match the switch to your generator's largest 240-volt outlet. A generator with an L14-30 outlet pairs with a 30-amp switch, such as the Reliance 31406CRK or 31410CRK. A generator with a 50-amp, 125/250-volt outlet can use a 50-amp inlet and a switch or interlock breaker sized for it. Then choose six or ten circuits based on how many essential loads you have.

faqs.q: Is there a transfer switch for just a furnace?
faqs.a: Yes. Single-circuit furnace transfer switches such as the Reliance TF151W mount at the furnace and let it run from either its normal circuit or a generator. They suit small or 120-volt-only generators, because a gas or oil furnace needs only a few hundred watts. Have an electrician confirm it suits your furnace, since some furnace controls are sensitive to generator grounding and polarity.

faqs.q: What is a generator inlet box?
faqs.a: A generator inlet box is a weatherproof box mounted on an outside wall with a male inlet where the generator cord plugs in. It is wired to the transfer switch or interlock breaker inside. The Reliance PB30 takes a 30-amp L14-30 cord and the PBN50 takes a 50-amp cord. It lets you connect the generator without running cords through a window or door, which would let exhaust indoors.

faqs.q: Will a transfer switch work with an inverter generator?
faqs.a: It depends on the generator's outlets. Many inverter generators are 120-volt only, which cannot properly feed a standard 120/240-volt switch or run any 240-volt load. Larger inverter models with an L14-30 outlet work with a 30-amp switch like any other generator. For a small 120-volt inverter, a single-circuit furnace switch is often the better match. Ask your electrician before connecting anything.
